beats.trigger: ## From Personal to Team
beats.got: Nothing new. This is the module title, and the topic is the one I came for.

beats.trigger: You can't really share an agent. You can share its context, a skill, its output or an interface, and choosing between them is a strategy decision.
beats.got: There are four things I can hand over, and picking one is a decision rather than a default.

beats.trigger: Bring one example from your own organisation of access without use: a tool people can open and mostly don't.
beats.got: I have an example, the Copilot rollout most of my team ignores. It's homework, so no reaction yet.

beats.trigger: **Find** the absorption bottleneck and draft a technical plan and a people plan side by side
beats.got: Nothing new. It's a list of verbs. The people plan beside the technical plan is the only part that interests me.

beats.trigger: What would you want a teammate to actually have: your folder, one of your skills, the morning output, or a way to ask it a question in Slack? And why that one?
beats.got: I'd say the output, because it needs no setup from them, but my folder problem comes up here too. That is the real question for my fourteen.

beats.trigger: You are not going to ask *"what should I share with my teammate?"* That question is builder-centered
beats.got: Start from the teammate's job, not my tool. Fair enough, but it's a lot of framing for a point I'd have made in one line. The Christensen and JTBD name-drop adds nothing.

beats.trigger: does it name one teammate, their current way of doing the job, and an outcome you could observe?
beats.got: I get a test for whether the JTBD file is specific. The warning about the agent ranging too wide or finishing too fast is useful. The file only counts if it names one person.

beats.trigger: If the reason is merely *"we already have the platform,"* send it back.
beats.got: Pick the sharing form for the outcome, not because the infrastructure allows it. I know that mistake and the CFO would catch it. Having the four options named is useful.

beats.trigger: You now have the teammate's job and a candidate selected against it.
beats.got: Nothing new. It's a handoff note to the next exercise.

beats.trigger: Now find the obstacle that decides whether the teammate can actually absorb it, then draft both halves of the plan.
beats.got: Nothing new. It restates the two files and the next step.

beats.trigger: A good bottleneck explains why several other obstacles stay hard.
beats.got: One load-bearing obstacle beats a list of six. That is how I'd want to brief my team, and I don't normally do it that way.

beats.trigger: A polished technical file beside a people file full of unnamed roles is the finding, not a finished rollout.
beats.got: I always write the technical side and leave 'who owns this' vague, and the agent will show that gap to me. The part where it doesn't invent names is good, because I'd distrust a made-up owner.

beats.trigger: checks the assumptions underneath these plans, imagines the failure, and writes the first real-world contact to `module-7/monday.md`.
beats.got: Nothing new. It's another handoff.

beats.trigger: The technical and people plans are hypotheses.
beats.got: The plans are guesses until I test them. I agree, and it's short enough.

beats.trigger: *what would have to be true for this teammate, doing this job, to fire their current hire and use my candidate?*
beats.got: This is the best question so far. It reads like a consulting question, and my CFO would respect it. I'd get two or three tests I could run this week.

beats.trigger: Six months from now, the teammate went back to the incumbent.
beats.got: The premortem pushes me to pick the most likely failure and act on it, ending in one person, one question and one test. That is concrete.

beats.trigger: A candidate picked because it fits the infrastructure is shopping. A candidate picked because it moves the outcome is design.
beats.got: Nothing new. It repeats the point from the pick step in neat slogan form. I got it the first time.

beats.trigger: Sharing an agent runs into one law.
beats.got: Nothing yet. 'One law' is bigger than I'd want to claim, but I'll wait to see what it is.

beats.trigger: Accountability is the part with a name on it, and a name does not travel inside a folder.
beats.got: Context, boundary and checks copy easily, but accountability stays with whoever built it. That explains my folder problem. If I hand out my context files, I'm still the one answering for them.

beats.trigger: The person who wants your folder is rarely the person who wants a Slack bot.
beats.got: Mostly nothing new. These are the same four strategies again, now sorted by who receives them. Only the one line about folder versus Slack bot was new, and my team of fourteen is a mix.

beats.trigger: Access is a switch somebody flips, and it completes in a minute.
beats.got: Nothing new. Access versus absorption is already in the title and the prework, and this says it a third time.

beats.trigger: Then name what would have had to change in people's weeks for them to use it.
beats.got: I'm to turn the unused-Copilot example into a list of what should have changed in people's weeks. It's a useful lens, but it's a task for me to do later.

beats.trigger: The leadership had not done the analysis. People they trusted had.
beats.got: Leadership needs to do some of the analysis themselves, or the work dies when priorities shift. That could happen to my pricing proposal, since the CFO and CEO won't have worked through it. The story is someone else's company, and its scale (millions of customers, fifteen contributors) isn't mine. The last two lines ('Who knows about the future') are a shrug.

beats.trigger: Somebody they trust has to have used it first and said so.
beats.got: Every job already has a current solution, and my candidate competes with that. The conditions to switch are small: it lands where they already look, it's right the first time, and a trusted colleague vouches for it. I can use these directly.

beats.trigger: Ask the question before you show them anything you built.
beats.got: Send one person one message and ask how they do the job now, before showing them anything. It's small enough that I will do it.

beats.trigger: Compare your choice with a neighbour's, then run the debrief.
beats.got: Nothing new. I'm told to compare with the person next to me, which will be pleasant but doesn't move my pricing work.

beats.trigger: Access is a switch someone flips. Absorption happens in other people's weeks, at their pace, for their reasons.
beats.got: Nothing new. It's a summary of what I've just done, and the access/absorption line is the fourth time.

beats.trigger: One real conversation tells you more about absorption than a finished plan does.
beats.got: I'm to bring back one real conversation and one test result. It's a reasonable accountability hook.

beats.trigger: In Module 8 you ask what changes when you don't have to build each one by hand.
beats.got: Nothing new. It's a teaser for the next module.

take_homes: Before I share anything with the team, I should find out what job one specific person is trying to get done, then pick context, skill, push or pull against that outcome. Fitting the tooling doesn't count as a reason.
A sharing plan needs a people plan with named owners. My files can be copied, but accountability stays with me unless I hand it over on purpose. Gaps in the plan should stay visible.
Ask what would have to be true for them to stop using what they do now. Test that before building more.

monday.move: Message one person on my team who feeds the pricing working group. Ask for twenty minutes on how they put together the pilot-cohort numbers today. Don't show them anything I've built. Then run the 'what would have to be true' question on their answer.
monday.who: One of my fourteen, probably the one who rebuilds the cohort brief by hand each time.
monday.when: Send the message Monday morning and have the conversation by Wednesday, ahead of the pricing working group.
monday.stop_condition: If their answer shows my brief doesn't change what they decide, I stop pushing it. If they'd use it only if it landed in the place they already look, I switch to push or pull before I build anything else.
monday.blocker: My team has no shared place for the context files and everyone keeps their own copy. So I can't hand over the context option yet, and the owner for that shared place is still unassigned.

misconception.why: The module never mentions prompts. It treats sharing as context, accountability and what the teammate does in their week. That moves my attention from writing better prompts to whether anyone will actually use the thing, but the module didn't confront the prompts idea directly, so I'd say shaken, not changed.

one_line: It's a good way to stop me building something clever and handing it out, and the bottleneck, people-plan and 'what would have to be true' bits were worth it, but it says 'access isn't absorption' about four times.
